description_full: Cadence Design Systems, Inc. develops computational, AI-driven software, hardware, and silicon intellectual property products and solutions. The company offers functional verification services, such as Jasper, a formal verification platform; Xcelium, a parallel logic simulation platform; Verisium, a generative AI solution; Palladium, an enterprise emulation platform; and Protium, a prototyping platform for chip verification, as well as digital IC design and sign off products, including Innovus platform; and custom IC design and simulation product include Virtuoso, a platform to design and verify analog. It also provides Xcelium logic simulator and other front-end verification and virtual prototyping technologies; controllers and physical interfaces; PCI Express, universal accelerator and compute express links, and multiple memory interfaces; and Tensilica, a digital signal processor. In addition, the company's design IP portfolio includes serializer/deserializer, peripheral component interconnect, USB, and other standard protocols; and Secure-IC, a solution for embedded security IP. Additionally, it provides System Design and Analysis (SD&A) platform, a solution that enables end-to-end system-level design and verification across chips, packages, PCBs, and electronic systems; Allegro X and Orca X platforms for PCB and advanced packaging; Sigrity X for signal and power integrity; AIR for RF design; Fidelity for computational fluid dynamics; Celsius for thermal and airflow analysis; Clarity 3D solver for electromagnetic and power electronics analysis and simulation; Integrity 3D-IC solution for 3D-IC and multi-chiplet designs; the Optimality Intelligent System Explorer, Reality digital twin, and Millennium enterprise multiphasic platforms; Allegro system design platform; and molecular modeling and simulation solutions and services. The company has a strategic collaboration with NVIDIA. The company was incorporated in 1987 and is headquartered in San Jose, California.

financial_summary: Cadence Design Systems, Inc. is a large-cap technology business with a $88.6B market cap on $5.3B of annual revenue.

The top line has compounded at +14% over the past three years and +12% annually across the full decade, the kind of sustained demand persistence that marks a compounder. Operating margins are expanding by +2.1pp year-over-year, which is one of the strongest signals that the moat is deepening.
Returns on capital run at 49% against a 11% cost of capital — a 38-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat.

The business throws off $1.6B in free cash flow — roughly 30 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.56× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and interest coverage of 13× is fortress-like.
Shareholder yield is only 0.9%, a thin return of capital, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome.

Antitrust and platform-regulation risk — the larger the network effect, the larger the regulatory target on its back, and a single consent decree can reset the moat.
AI disruption of existing software moats — incumbents with durable margins face commoditisation as AI-native competitors replicate features at a fraction of the R&D cost.
Cybersecurity liability and talent cost inflation — a single breach can erase years of goodwill, and the war for engineering talent compresses margins even at scale.

sect: Its 28% operating margin runs 21pp above the Technology median (7%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
Its share of sector profits slightly exceeds its share of revenue (1.20x).
It accounts for 0.1% of sector revenue and 0.1% of sector operating profit.
Over five years it has been gaining share of the sector profit pool (+1.3% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 533 companies in the universe; the top four hold 29% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares have drifted higher, up 6% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 22% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 42% and a beta of 1.28, it amplifies market moves.
Liquidity is deep, with about $708.4M traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 32% in the 2020 crash, 26% in the 2022 bear market and 84% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $135 (margin of safety -140%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 46%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $89.92 to $213 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Technology peers: P/E 64.2 vs 27.4, EV/EBITDA 41.8 vs 17.1 and P/FCF 55.8 vs 26.1 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 24% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 1.8% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 1.6% (vs the 8% bar).
The 24 covering analysts target $412 on average, 27% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 49% clears the cost of capital of 10.8% by 38pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.78).
It converts 30% of revenue into free cash flow, or 21% after stock compensation.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.56x.
ROE of 20% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.9x equity multiplier).
It spends 8.6% of revenue on stock compensation (above the 2% gate).
hlth: The balance sheet carries net cash of $3.2B (4% of market cap).
growth: Revenue has compounded at 14.1% over 3 years, 14.6% over 5 years and 12.0% over 10 years.
At current returns, reinvesting 28% of profits supports about 13.7% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Free cash flow has compounded 14.4% a year over five years.
Forward indicators: a book-to-bill of 1.19 (orders outpacing sales), a backlog worth 1.5x annual revenue and deferred revenue up 10%.
Capex runs only 0.6x depreciation (2.7% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.3%), and institutions hold 91%.
Insiders have only sold over the past year (15 sales, net $2.7M sold).
Shareholder yield is a modest 0.9% (0.9% in buybacks).
The share count has shrunk 0.6% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
people: With about 13,800 employees, each generates about $384K of revenue, in line with the Technology median, and revenue has grown 12.2% a year across its filed history.
That works out to $115K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $2.3M (6x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (3/10, lower is better).
